name: Ojibwe, southeastern
confidence_why: Valentine 1996 and Newell & Piggott 2006 (Ottawa data) both describe quantity-sensitive iambic feet built from the left edge with the final syllable often left unfooted, and the only disagreements are over detail: whether main stress sits in the antepenultimate foot (Kaye 1973, Piggott 1983) or the penultimate foot (Hayes 1995, Piggott 2004), Rhodes 1976's remark that the prominence is pitch rather than stress, and Chamberlain 1892's nineteenth-century note that accent follows no fixed rule.
catalog_citation: Valentine, J. Randolph. 1996. Phonological parameters of Ojibwe dialect variation. In David H. Pentland (ed.), Papers of the 27th Algonquian Conference, 287-323. Winnipeg: University of Manitoba. Open copy:https://ojs.library.carleton.ca/index.php/ALGQP/article/download/539/441
catalog_quote: STRESS. The stress system of Ojibwe has been analyzed by a number of researchers (Bloomfield 1958, Rhodes 1976, Valentine 1985, etc.). Basically, the system is one of quantity sensitive iambic feet built from the left edge of the word, i.e., a preferred rhythm of weak-strong, in which the weak position may only be filled by a short vowel. The final syllable is often analyzed as extrametrical. Very similar stress systems have been proposed for other Algonquian languages, e.g., Passamaquoddy (Stowell 1979). In southeastern dialects of Ojibwe, a very prominent rule of weak vowel syncope is resulting in a restructuring of much of the lexicon and the form of inflectional person prefixes on verbs and nouns. In other dialects, such as Berens River Ojibwe, the same quantity-sensitive iambic metrical patterns are evident, but the correlate of stress in these dialects is pitch, resulting in alternations of high and low tones on stressed and unstressed vowels (see Fiero 1964, Valentine 1987). ... Some dialects show clear evidence of stress shifts, as well, particularly with words that consist only of short vowels. (pp. 312-313)
world_status: statement found in an open source
sweep_summary: Eastern Ojibwa (east2542) is not in the catalog. this search of works with stress in the title had a single title item, Glottolog ref 688395 'Stress in Border Lakes Ojibwe' (2003), which Glottolog lists author-less under the volume editor H.C. Wolfart and tags with language code east2542. The Carleton OJS landing page (article 413) identifies the author as Bonnie Swierzbin (Papers of the 34th Algonquian Conference, pp. 341-370); the open PDF was downloaded fromhttps://ojs.library.carleton.ca/index.php/ALGQP/article/download/413/317The paper is an instrumental study of Border Lakes Ojibwe, a NON-syncopating dialect on the Ontario-Minnesota border (Seine River consultants), which the author calls a 'southern dialect' and Glottolog geography places under Northwestern Ojibwa (nort2961/rain1239) - it is not Eastern Ojibwa, so the Glottolog language tag is a misassignment. Its findings (p. 367): iambs left-to-right, no degenerate feet, binary right-headed cola, primary stress on the rightmost non-final heavy syllable except HH' words. Its only statements about Eastern Ojibwa/Odawa are second-hand (Kaye 1973, Piggott 1980/1983, Hayes 1995; pp. 357-358: Odawa primary stress on the penultimate stressed vowel with two stressed vowels, antepenultimate with three or more). No first-hand Eastern Ojibwa stress statement was read in this search of works with stress in the title (no new stress statement was found); our earlier reading's Valentine 1996 / Rhodes 1976 / Chamberlain 1892 / SPA-1979-on-Bloomfield material in the same folder remains the best. Nothing to acquire from this search of works with stress in the title (priority none). for the session was exhausted; lookups were done by automated download against Glottolog and Carleton OJS.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Quantity-sensitive iambic feet are built left to right from the start of the word: a short-vowel syllable is weak and the next syllable is strong; a long-vowel syllable is always strong (it can never be the weak member); the final syllable is treated as extrametrical. Strong syllables are stressed, weak ones unstressed; in Eastern Ojibwa/Odawa (the 'southeastern dialects') the weak short vowels are syncopated. Valentine 1996 does not say which strong syllable carries primary word stress; for Odawa, Piggott 1980/1983 and Kaye 1973 (via Chambers 1979 and Swierzbin 2003) put it on the antepenultimate stressed syllable in words with three or more stressed vowels, otherwise on the first (penultimate) stressed one.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not separated from primary stress in Valentine 1996: every foot head (each long vowel and each even-numbered short vowel counting from the left) is prominent; the Odawa literature (Piggott 1983 pp. 81-83) treats all such syllables plus the word-final syllable as stressed, with one of them promoted to main stress.
new_statements.exceptions: Final syllable extrametrical; northern dialects (e.g. Severn) show stress shifts in sequences of short vowels; Berens River uses pitch rather than intensity as the correlate; Piggott notes CVNCV disyllables with initial stress in Odawa; Chamberlain 1892 (Mississauga of Scugog) reported no fixed accent rule and 'practically no accent' in most disyllables.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level, isolation forms; the statement is made for Ojibwe as a whole (all dialects) and explicitly extends to the syncopating southeastern dialects that include Eastern Ojibwa; the SPA 1979 database entry for Eastern Ojibwa (reading Bloomfield 1957) states that Bloomfield does not mention word stress but describes reduction of short vowels in odd-numbered non-final syllables, which is the same iambic pattern.
new_statements.identity_note: The quoted Valentine 1996 statement is made for Ojibwe as a whole (all dialects, Glottolog nuclear-Ojibwe group cent2252 and beyond) and applies to Eastern Ojibwa as one of the 'southeastern dialects' with weak-vowel syncope; it is not a description of east2542 alone. The primary-stress placement (antepenultimate stressed syllable) comes only from the Odawa literature (Kaye 1973, Piggott 1980/1983; otta1242, already in the catalog), and Valentine 2001 treats Odawa and Eastern Ojibwe together as Nishnaabemwin. Chamberlain 1892 describes the Mississauga (Scugog) variety of Eastern Ojibwa; Rhodes 1976 (diss.) calls the Walpole Island / Wikwemikong dialect 'Central Ojibwa' but identifies it with Bloomfield's Eastern Ojibwa.

new_statements.quote: The location of stressed syllables is determined by a left-to-right parsing of syllables into iambic feet, with one of the stressed syllables promoted to primary stress status. Postulating that final syllables are always stressed, Kaye (1973) and Piggott (1980b, 1983) describe the invariable locus of primary stress as the antepenultimate foot in words containing more than two feet. [...] In contrast, Hayes (1995:218) argues for the possibility that, at least in some cases, final syllables are phonetically prominent but not necessarily stressed. Such a hypothesis yields an analysis in which the location of primary stress varies between the penultimate and antepenultimate foot.

new_statements.relation_note: Agrees with the catalog's/Valentine 1996's left-to-right quantity-sensitive iambic footing and adds the primary-stress placement (antepenultimate or penultimate foot, depending on the analysis of final syllables), the prosodic-word domain (whole verb complex) and the treatment of final syllables. Caveat: fn. 2 (p. 269) states 'The data here represent the Ottawa dialect of Ojibwe', i.e. Odawa (otta1242), the sister syncopating variety, not Eastern Ojibwa proper; the paper otherwise speaks of 'Ojibwe' generally.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Syllables are parsed left to right into iambic feet (the PDF's own examples in (26) treat a final syllable as stressed only if it is heavy or part of a disyllabic foot, i.e. weight matters); every foot head is stressed, and one foot head is promoted to primary stress: the antepenultimate foot in words of more than two feet under Kaye 1973 / Piggott 1980b, 1983 (final syllables always stressed), or the penultimate-or-antepenultimate foot under Hayes 1995; fn. 9 p. 283 reports Piggott 2004, in which all final syllables are unfooted and unstressed and 'the main stress syllable can be invariably located within the penultimate foot'. The authors do not choose between these descriptions. The domain is the whole verb complex (tense prefixes and preverbs can carry main stress, p. 284), and 'the most prominent syllable in a word may be followed by no more than two stressed syllables' (p. 284).
new_statements.secondary_stress: Every iambic foot head is a stressed syllable; only one is promoted to primary stress (pp. 282-283). The paper marks only the most prominent syllable (acute accent) in its examples.
new_statements.exceptions: Degenerate (monomoraic) feet are tolerated only at the right edge of a phase (pp. 288-289); fn. 8 (p. 281): the short second vowel of a V-V sequence is unstressed and subject to optional, rate-dependent deletion.
new_statements.identity_note: Newell & Piggott 2006 describes the Ottawa (Odawa, otta1242) dialect of Ojibwe per its fn. 2, i.e. the sister syncopating 'Nishnaabemwin' variety rather than Eastern Ojibwa proper, though its statements are phrased for 'Ojibwe' generally. Bowers 2019 concerns Nishnaabemwin (the cover term for Odawa and Eastern Ojibwa together). Rhodes 1985 covers Eastern Ojibwa, Chippewa and Ottawa.

new_statements.quote: Bloomfield reported that “the vowels of [. . . ] odd-numbered” light syllables were reduced, where the count goes from left to right, restarts after long vowels, and ignores the final syllable (Bloomfield 1957:5). The alternating reduction matches the uncontroversial iambic stress pattern common in Ojibwe dialects (Valentine 1994), which places odd-numbered light syllables in the weak branch of the foot. Specifically, the typical Ojibwe dialect has iteratively assigned left-aligned iambs, with otherwise unparseable final syllables placed in a degenerate foot. While syllables with long vowels are always heavy, closed syllables are not.

new_statements.relation_note: Same system as the catalog record and existing statements (Valentine 1996: quantity-sensitive iambic feet built from the left edge, weak position only a short vowel; Newell & Piggott 2006: left-to-right iambic parsing): Bowers restates it as 'uncontroversial' for Ojibwe dialects and adds detail - long vowels heavy but closed syllables not, degenerate final foot (rather than extrametrical final syllable), count restarts after long vowels, person prefixes inside the footing domain - and adds the diachronic point that in modern Nishnaabemwin (Odawa/Eastern Ojibwe, post-1930's) the weak vowels are deleted so there is no longer a prominence contrast between unstressed and secondarily stressed sy…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Ojibwe dialects, including 1930's Nishnaabemwin (Odawa/Eastern Ojibwe), have quantity-sensitive iambic feet assigned iteratively from the left edge of the word: a light (short-vowel) syllable in odd position sits in the weak branch and the following syllable is stressed; syllables with long vowels are always heavy (they head their own foot and the light-syllable count restarts after them), closed syllables do not count as heavy; a leftover word-final syllable forms a degenerate (stressed) foot; person prefixes are inside the footing domain, so prefixation shifts which stem vowels are weak. Bloomfield's 1930's severe reduction targeted exactly the weak (odd-numbered light) vowels; in modern Nishnaabemwin those vowels are deleted (restructured URs on Bowers's analysis). The paper does not say which foot carries primary stress.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Every foot head is marked as stressed in the 1930's transcriptions (e.g. [(2nÍ)(SIná:)(bÉ:)(mUwÍn)]), i.e. iterative rhythmic stresses; fn. 1 (ms p. 3, p. 4): 'Stress is marked for transcriptions of 1930’s forms, but not for subsequent reanalyses or restructured forms, since with the loss of unstressed syllables, there is no prominence contrast between unstressed and secondarily stressed syllables.' No statement of primary vs secondary stress placement.
new_statements.exceptions: Closed syllables are not heavy (only long vowels are); the final syllable is 'ignored' by the reduction count / parsed as a degenerate foot and never reduced; the iambic count restarts after a long vowel (sec. 2.3, ms p. 7: 'Because the stress algorithm “restarted” the iambic stress pattern after a long vowel, the person prefix only affected the footing of the stem-initial vowel'); person prefixes are footed with the stem. For the modern variety, sec. 7.1 argues 'There is no need for the grammar to build and destroy iambic feet' because syncopated vowels are absent from URs (restructuring), against Valentine's (2001) recapitulationist stress-plus-syncope analysis (sec. 7.2).
new_statements.identity_note: The work treats Nishnaabemwin, 'a collective name for the Odawa and Eastern Ojibwe dialects of Ojibwe' (ms p. 1), i.e. it covers both east2542 (Eastern Ojibwe) and Odawa/Ottawa (otta1242); the stress description is explicitly given for 'the typical Ojibwe dialect' and for 1930's Nishnaabemwin as documented by Bloomfield (1957, Eastern Ojibwa/Odawa of Walpole Island speaker). Modern (post-1930's) Nishnaabemwin has deleted the unstressed vowels.

readall_conflicts: No contradiction between what was opened and the catalog. Newell & Piggott 2006 (Ottawa data) agrees with Valentine 1996's pan-Ojibwe quantity-sensitive iambic footing from the left edge and adds the primary-stress placement, but it reports a disagreement in the literature about where primary stress lands within the foot sequence: antepenultimate foot if final syllables count as stressed (Kaye 1973; Piggott 1980b, 1983), penultimate or antepenultimate foot if final syllables are only phonetically prominent (Hayes 1995:218), or invariably the penultimate foot if final syllables are unfooted (Piggott 2004, fn. 9). Bowers 2019 (abstract only) and Rhodes 1985 (not opened) add nothing that conflicts. Earlier passes in hold two second-hand notes that sit uneasily beside the iambic account: Chamberlain 1892 (Mississauga of Scugog) says accent varies 'at the caprice of the speaker', and Rhodes 1976 (fn., p. 155) calls the prominence pitch or pitch accent rather than stress; neither was among the three works assigned here.

tone.quote: Many of the languages have alternating stress patterns. … In terms of metrical stress theory (Hayes 1995), this is a quantity-sensitive left-to-right iambic pattern. Similar left-to-right iambic patterns are found in Menominee, Ojibwe, Potawatomi, and Delaware, and right-to-left iambic patterns are reported for Meskwaki and Cree … Contrastive tone has developed in Cheyenne, Kickapoo, and Western Innu; pitch accent systems, sometimes described as tonal, have developed in Blackfoot, Arapaho, Maliseet-Passamaquoddy, and Penobscot.
tone.locator: author's preprint p. 6, section 2.5 'Stress and tone' (published chapter pp. 504-523)
tone.says: A survey of Algonquian lists Ojibwe among the languages with left-to-right iambic stress; contrastive tone and pitch accent are reported only for other Algonquian languages, not for Ojibwe. (statement read as group-level, not specific to this language).
